source.title: Open Problems on Information and Feedback Controlled Systems

accepted.question_text: For a feedback-controlled dynamical system, how large can the performance gain be when the controller has access to a specified amount of information about the system state? Equivalently, what quantitative upper bounds relate available information to achievable improvements in performance measures such as extracted work, efficiency, power output, or flux?

evidence.quote: Therefore, the first natural main question is how much the performance can be increased with a certain amount of information, or, stated otherwise, which are the bounds of the performance increase.

accepted.question_text: How can one formulate the thermodynamics of feedback-controlled systems in a way that explicitly accounts for the thermodynamic consequences of information transfer between the system and the controller, so that quantities such as entropy reduction, extractable work, and efficiency are treated within a consistent thermodynamic framework?

evidence.quote: The second main question is the establishment of the thermodynamics of feedback controlled systems accounting for thermodynamic effects of the information transfer.

accepted.question_text: For correlated repeated actuation of a feedback controller, what is the precise relationship between the entropy-reduction results derived from the viewpoint of the controlled system and Zurek's algorithmic-complexity analysis of the combined system-plus-controller, especially regarding the minimum energetic cost of erasing the controller's stored measurement record and the resulting thermodynamic limits on the system's entropy reduction?

evidence.quote: One particular open question involves the precise relations between these recent results and the algorithmic complexity approach adopted by Zurek [6, 7] to study the correlated repeated actuation of a feedback controller from the perspective of the system plus controller.

This study has allowed Zurek to establish the minimum energetic cost for erasing a memory that has stored the measurements the controller has processed (see Section II A). This minimum energetic cost also sets thermodynamic constraints that lead to a maximum entropy reduction for the system.

accepted.question_text: Can the entropy-reduction results obtained for correlated repeated feedback actuation be applied or extended to derive quantitative bounds for additional performance measures of feedback-controlled systems, in particular the maximum attainable flux or the maximum attainable power?

evidence.quote: Another open question is the application or the extension of the results found in [13] to find bounds for other performance measures of feedback controlled systems, for example, the maximum attainable flux or power.

accepted.question_text: When a feedback controller acts continuously, meaning that its actuation period is shorter than every characteristic time scale of the system dynamics, how can the results obtained for discrete repeated feedback actuation be extended to this continuous-time limit despite the nontrivial relation between discrete entropy and differential entropy?

evidence.quote: Therefore, even the extension of the results in [13] to the continuous actuation limit remains still an open problem.

Continuous actuation of the feedback controller is effectively present when the controller repeatedly actuates on the system with a period shorter than any of the characteristic time scales of the system dynamics.

accepted.question_text: For feedback-controlled flashing ratchets, can the general thermodynamic results of [13] be applied to determine the maximum entropy reduction these ratchets can achieve and to establish a full thermodynamic description of such systems?

evidence.quote: The application of the results of [13] to feedback controlled flashing ratchets has not been done yet.

It will allow to establish bounds on the entropy reduction attainable for feedback flashing ratchet and to establish the thermodynamics of these systems, which are theoretically and technologically relevant. Therefore, this is another relevant open problem.

accepted.question_text: The known bounds for feedback flashing ratchets express flux improvement and power improvement in terms of the information used per actuation. How can these bounds be reformulated in terms of the total non-redundant information acquired per unit time, so that the ratchet results can be related directly to the entropy-reduction and thermodynamic framework developed for general feedback-controlled systems?

evidence.quote: These relation were stated in terms of the information per actuation. However, how to restate these relations in terms of the total amount of information per unit time (i.e., only computing non-redundant information per unit time) is still an open question.
This restatement will help to put these results [38, 39] in relation with those found in [13] for the entropy reduction and the thermodynamics of a general feedback controlled system.

accepted.question_text: What concrete limitations do information-theoretic and thermodynamic bounds for feedback-controlled systems impose on the operation and achievable performance of nanotechnology devices and biological systems in which one subsystem uses bidirectional interaction with another subsystem to improve that subsystem's performance?
accepted.context_brief: Implications for nano and biological systems

evidence.quote: Thus, the bounds of the performance of the feedback controlled systems will imply limitations to the operation of nanotechnology devices and biological systems. Finding these implications is still a very relevant open question.

trace.notes: Resolved the arXiv abs URL to a local PDF and mapped the document structure from the parsed PDF text. The open-problem material is concentrated in Section III on pages 6-8, with subsections on general feedback-controlled systems, flashing ratchets, and nanotechnology/biological systems.
Extracted eight explicit open-question statements from Section III, including the two main questions in Section III.A and the more specific problems in subsections III.A.1, III.A.2, III.B, and III.C.
Expanded the paper's main performance-bound question into a self-contained formulation that names representative performance measures mentioned across the paper.
Rewrote the thermodynamics question to state explicitly that the issue is building a consistent thermodynamic framework incorporating information transfer.
Resolved the cross-reference to Zurek's approach using the surrounding source text on the same page about erasure cost and entropy reduction.
Kept the target performance measures explicit by carrying forward the source examples of flux and power.
Made the continuous-actuation limit self-contained by inlining the paper's definition of continuous actuation and the discrete-versus-differential entropy obstacle.
Rewrote the flashing-ratchet problem as a concrete application of the general thermodynamic results in reference [13].
Expanded the compressed statement about per-actuation information into a self-contained question about non-redundant information rate per unit time.
Rewrote the final open question to identify the relevant class of systems as nanotechnology devices and biological systems with feedback-like bidirectional interactions.

Reviewed the extracted candidates and kept eight distinct questions; the two broad Section III.A questions were retained separately from their more specific follow-on questions because they ask at different levels of generality.
All accepted items are self-contained, evidence-backed with page citations from the PDF, and do not rely on unresolved section references or unsupported technical additions.
